entries.reason: read CLASS-SCOPED with tools/corpus/objc-inventory.lua over the armv7 caches of 6.1.3 and 4.3, ABSENT at both, controls as the MPMusicPlayerQueueDescriptor row records. New code, so nothing to shadow. ITS DESCRIPTOR IS REAL BECAUSE THE RELEASE'S OWN MPMusicPlayerController CAN CONSUME IT, read at CLASS level: that class is PRESENT at both ends with 66 own instance and 5 own class methods at 6.1.3 and 52 and 5 at 4.3, and among the 66 are -setQueueWithQuery: and -setQueueWithItemCollection:, both declared PUBLIC by the SDK header, plus -setQueueWithQuery:firstItem:, -setQueueWithSeedItems: and -setQueueWithGeniusMixPlaylist:. So this descriptor's query and itemCollection map onto a setter the release really has, at the release's own argument order, and the queue the caller then reads back through -nowPlayingItemAtIndex: is the release's own. WHAT IS NOT USED IS AS DELIBERATE AS WHAT IS: the release also has -setQueueWithQuery:firstItem:, which is exactly the call this descriptor's startItem wants, but NO SDK HEADER DECLARES IT - the public queue setters in the 16.4 header are -setQueueWithQuery:, -setQueueWithItemCollection:, -setQueueWithStoreIDs:, -setQueueWithDescriptor:, -prependQueueDescriptor: and -appendQueueDescriptor:, and the two-argument form is not among them - so it is a PRIVATE framework method and this port does not call it. The per-item time windows are keyed by the item's persistentID, and MPMediaEntityPersistentID is uint64_t in BOTH SDKs (MPMediaEntity.h:15 in 16.4 and in 26.2); an item with a zero persistent ID is declined rather than keyed by object address, which would make the window unreachable on the next call
entries.effect: NSClassFromString answers the class; a descriptor built with -initWithQuery: or -initWithItemCollection: holds what it was given, with the query COPIED because the header declares that property `copy`, and -[MPMusicPlayerController setQueueWithDescriptor:] hands it to the release's own -setQueueWithQuery: or -setQueueWithItemCollection:. A startItem is held but not applied, for the private-selector reason the row gives

THE MEASUREMENT THAT DECIDES THE DIFFERENCE FROM ITS SIBLING is at class level on MPMusicPlayerController's own 66 instance methods at 6.1.3 and 52 at 4.3: neither -setQueueWithStoreIDs: nor -setQueueWithItemIDs: is among them, while the two media-item setters are. So a store queue on this device would have no items at all. -[MPMusicPlayerController setQueueWithDescriptor:] therefore leaves the queue alone for this subclass rather than fabricating a query out of Store IDs, which would be a different API's answer under this method's name, and -[MPMusicPlayerControllerMutableQueue insertQueueDescriptor:afterItem:] inserts nothing rather than appearing to succeed

Nothing on this release resolves the IDs to items, so the queue setters leave the queue alone for it - which is the honest answer and not a missing one

entries.reason: THE RELEASE'S OWN METHOD LIST IS WHAT MAKES THIS A BRIDGE. Read at CLASS level with tools/corpus/objc-inventory.lua over the armv7 cache of 6.1.3, MPMusicPlayerController is PRESENT with 66 own instance methods, and -setQueueWithQuery: and -setQueueWithItemCollection: are among them; both are declared PUBLIC by the SDK header. The release's own -setQueueWithDescriptor: is absent from its 66 - the SDK declares it at 10.1 and the release predates that - so this is the port's category supplying the spelling, and it translates rather than rebuilds: a descriptor holding a query goes to -setQueueWithQuery:, one holding an item collection to -setQueueWithItemCollection:, each the release's own method with the release's own single argument. The caller then hears its queue back through the release's own -nowPlayingItemAtIndex:. The 0 count that would have mattered is not used: the whole-cache selector list (113981 DISTINCT NAMES) would have said some class somewhere declares these, and the per-class read above is what decides a member. NOT BRIDGED, AND NOT A GAP IN THIS ROW: a Store-ID descriptor calls nothing, because neither -setQueueWithStoreIDs: nor -setQueueWithItemIDs: is in the release's 66 at either held end and MPMediaItem.playbackStoreID is on 0 of the 113981 names. The release's own -setQueueWithQuery:firstItem: is deliberately NOT called even though it is among the 66 and is exactly what a startItem needs, because no SDK header declares it and this port does not reach for a private framework method where a public one exists
entries.effect: a media-item descriptor sets the release's own queue, and the caller reads it back through the release's own accessors; a Store-ID descriptor and an empty descriptor leave the queue alone rather than setting one the caller did not ask for

entries.reason: read at CLASS level on MPMusicPlayerController's own 66 instance methods at 6.1.3 and 52 at 4.3, every queue setter the release has REPLACES the queue: -setQueueWithQuery:, -setQueueWithItemCollection:, -setQueueWithSeedItems:, -setQueueWithQuery:firstItem: and -setQueueWithGeniusMixPlaylist:. There is no append and no prepend, and no way to read the current queue as a value that could be re-set with one item added: -nowPlayingItem is the item being PLAYED and -nowPlayingItemAtIndex: indexes the release's queue by position, and neither returns the queue itself. So there is no release operation for this method to call, and the queue is left alone. The alternative - read the current queue, append in memory, call -setQueueWithQuery: with the result - would change which item plays next and lose the release's own start item, and the caller would then hear a queue through the release's accessors that the release never agreed to. The header's return type is void, so there is no error channel and nothing is invented to report through one. The check asserts that NO release setter is called, which is the claim that can be observed
entries.effect: nothing: the queue is left exactly as the caller had it, because the release has no operation that appends to one and reading the current queue is not something it offers

entries.reason: the same class-level read as the append row, and the same finding: all five queue setters MPMusicPlayerController has at 6.1.3 and 4.3 REPLACE the queue, and none appends or prepends, and neither -nowPlayingItem nor -nowPlayingItemAtIndex: returns the current queue as a value. So this method has no release operation to call and leaves the queue alone rather than re-setting a queue rebuilt in memory, which would change which item plays first and would be a queue the release never agreed to. Return type void, so no error channel exists and none is invented. The check asserts that no release setter is called

entries.reason: read CLASS-SCOPED with tools/corpus/objc-inventory.lua over the armv7 caches of 6.1.3 and 4.3, ABSENT at both, controls as the MPMusicPlayerQueueDescriptor row records. New code, so nothing to shadow, and it is the half of the 10.3 contract the release cannot do: -insertQueueDescriptor:afterItem: is a transaction-level insert, and every queue setter the release has REPLACES a queue rather than editing one. The header's own contract is honoured in the order it states: a nil afterItem means the front, and a named afterItem the queue does not hold is inserted at the front rather than at a guessed position. The items inserted are read through the release's OWN MPMediaQuery and MPMediaItemCollection accessors, and a Store-ID descriptor inserts NOTHING rather than appearing to succeed, for the reason the MPMusicPlayerStoreQueueDescriptor row gives. -removeItem: removes exactly the item it names and leaves the queue unchanged for one it does not hold
entries.effect: a transaction block is handed a mutable queue it can insert into and remove from, and the queue the completion handler is given is the one the block produced

entries.reason: read CLASS-SCOPED with tools/corpus/objc-inventory.lua over the armv7 caches of 6.1.3 and 4.3, ABSENT at both, controls as the MPMusicPlayerQueueDescriptor row records. New code, so nothing to shadow, and it is a real subclass of MPMusicPlayerController, which the release DOES have with 66 own instance and 5 own class methods at 6.1.3 - so what it inherits is the release's own play, pause and queue accessors rather than anything invented here. Its one declared method, -performQueueTransaction:completionHandler:, is a transaction: the block runs FIRST against a mutable queue and the handler is called after it, exactly once, with the queue the block produced and a nil error - and a nil error is the only honest value, because the two mutators a block can call are both void and both decline rather than report, so no operation in the transaction can fail. The queue it edits is the port's own value, because the release's queue is not readable as one
entries.effect: a caller runs a transaction against a mutable queue and is handed the resulting queue, with the release's own playback accessors available on the controller it is

entries.source: no SDK header declares it: grep for @interface MPSystemMusicPlayerController over the MediaPlayer headers of 16.4 and of 26.2 finds no file. The row is the method the queue names it for, -openToPlayQueueDescriptor:completionHandler:, MP_API(ios(11.0))
entries.reason: DECLARED BY NO SDK HEADER AT ALL - not in 16.4, not in 26.2 - and the release carries no such class: tools/corpus/objc-inventory.lua over the armv7 caches of 6.1.3 and 4.3 reads MPSystemMusicPlayerController ABSENT from both, with the controls in the same two files. It is declared and implemented here anyway, because the method row that names it is a real public row whose only spelling this class has, and a category cannot be written on a class that does not exist. TWO DEFECTS FOUND BY COMPILING IT, both of which are the kind a reader would not see: an @interface alone is not enough and leaves _OBJC_CLASS_$_MPSystemMusicPlayerController undefined at link time, measured as an Undefined symbols error naming the category; and a category on a class declared in the same file needs that class implemented too. The @implementation is EMPTY ON PURPOSE - the class is MPMusicPlayerController's system-music sibling, so what it can honestly be is what it inherits, the release's own playback accessors - and inventing a body would mean inventing what a system music player does on a release that has no such thing
entries.effect: NSClassFromString answers the class and it is a kind of MPMusicPlayerController, so it answers the release's own playback accessors; it declares no behaviour of its own beyond the one method below

entries.source: SDK 26.2 and the iPhoneOS16.4 SDK both declare it at MPMusicPlayerController.h:46, under the protocol MPSystemMusicPlayerController at :43, as - (void)openToPlayQueueDescriptor:(MPMusicPlayerQueueDescriptor *)queueDescriptor MP_API(ios(11.0), tvos(14.0)) MP_UNAVAILABLE(watchos, macos) NS_SWIFT_NAME(openToPlay(_:)); - one argument and no completion handler. The old source on this row carried the selector as the port spells it, -openToPlayQueueDescriptor:completionHandler:, which no SDK declares; that spelling is still answered at MPMusicPlayerControllerQueueDescriptor101.m, because an application already compiled against it links, but it is not the API this row names
entries.reason: the receiver is a class no SDK header declares as a class and no release carries - read ABSENT from both 6.1.3 and 4.3 with tools/corpus/objc-inventory.lua, controls as the MPSystemMusicPlayerController row records - so no application on this release can send it, and the method is answered because the port's own header surface names it and a caller compiling against the SDK's spelling must link. What it can honestly do is nothing: MPMusicPlayerController.h:44 says the method "Switches to Music to play the content provided by the queue descriptor", there is no Music application on this release to switch to and no system music player to play it, and the declaration takes no completion handler and returns void, so there is no channel to report a failure through and none is invented. That is the same reasoning -[MPMusicPlayerController appendQueueDescriptor:] and -prependQueueDescriptor: give, and the same answer

entries.reason: read CLASS-SCOPED with tools/corpus/objc-inventory.lua over the armv7 caches of 6.1.3 and 4.3, ABSENT at both, controls as the MPMusicPlayerQueueDescriptor row records. New code, so nothing to shadow. It is a typed wrapper around a dictionary and nothing more: the header's only initializer is - (nullable instancetype)initWithDictionary:(NSDictionary<NSString *, id> *)dictionary and its only property is '@property (nonatomic, readonly, copy) NSDictionary<NSString *, id> *dictionary', so the class IS the dictionary. The initializer is typed NULLABLE, which is Apple's own statement that it can decline, and it does: a nil dictionary produces nil rather than an object holding nothing, because the dictionary is the entire content of the class. Copied on the way in, because the property is `copy`
entries.effect: NSClassFromString answers the class; a caller-built object holds the dictionary it was given, copied, and -initWithDictionary:nil answers nil as the header's own nullability allows

entries.reason: read CLASS-SCOPED with tools/corpus/objc-inventory.lua over the armv7 caches of 6.1.3 and 4.3, ABSENT at both, controls as the MPMusicPlayerQueueDescriptor row records. New code, so nothing to shadow. It is the same shape as MPMusicPlayerMediaItemQueueDescriptor - an ordered queue plus a start entry plus two per-entry time setters - but the window is keyed by the entry's INDEX in the queue, because a play-parameters entry is a dictionary with no persistent ID of its own and a queue's entries are ordered; an entry that is not in the queue is declined rather than appended to the search, since a window recorded against an entry the queue cannot play names nothing. Its superclass is MPMusicPlayerQueueDescriptor, whose -init the header marks MP_INIT_UNAVAILABLE - a COMPILE-TIME attribute, MediaPlayerDefines.h:70-73 - so this initializer calls the named base initializer that object declares for exactly that purpose, measured as three 'init' is unavailable errors before the change
entries.effect: NSClassFromString answers the class; a descriptor holds the ordered play parameters it was built with, copied, and its two time setters record a window against an entry that is in the queue and decline one that is not

entries.source: no SDK header declares it; it is the port's own, and MP_INIT_UNAVAILABLE on MPMusicPlayerQueueDescriptor is why it exists
entries.reason: A SEAM THE PORT OWNS, registered because the registry check asks what is built and finds nothing otherwise - the rule AGENTS.md records after a reviewer's verdict on a helper that carried no release. It exists because MP_INIT_UNAVAILABLE is a COMPILE-TIME attribute: MediaPlayerDefines.h:70-73 expands it to '+ (instancetype)new NS_UNAVAILABLE; - (instancetype)init NS_UNAVAILABLE;', so a subclass initializer cannot call [super init] - measured, three 'init' is unavailable errors, one per initializer, before this was added. Both concrete subclasses of the base in this library call it instead: MPMusicPlayerMediaItemQueueDescriptor and MPMusicPlayerStoreQueueDescriptor here, and MPMusicPlayerPlayParametersQueueDescriptor from the 11.0 object. It is declared ONCE, on the base in this object, and the 11.0 object only uses it - restating the category in that file produced 'duplicate definition of category CharonSubclassInit on interface MPMusicPlayerQueueDescriptor', measured
entries.effect: the base's one initializer, reachable by the header's own concrete initializers; +new and -init stay unavailable exactly as the header writes them, and -init still refuses at runtime on the abstract base

entries.source: no SDK header declares it; it is the port's own, and MP_INIT_UNAVAILABLE on MPMusicPlayerControllerQueue is why it exists
entries.reason: A SEAM THE PORT OWNS, registered for the reason the row above gives. MPMusicPlayerControllerQueue is MP_INIT_UNAVAILABLE, so -[MPMusicPlayerApplicationController performQueueTransaction:completionHandler:] cannot build one with -init; it calls this instead, and the mutable subclass inherits it. The name begins with 'init' because it IS an initializer and the compiler enforces the init family: a first draft called it charonInitQueueWithItems: and clang rejected 'cannot assign to self outside of a method in the init family'. Its argument is the port's own queue value rather than the release's, because the release's queue is not readable as one - -nowPlayingItem is the item being played and -nowPlayingItemAtIndex: indexes it, and neither returns it - and an implementation that seeded this from the release's live queue would hand a caller a queue the release never produced
entries.effect: a queue is built from the port's own item array, copied, which is what a transaction and the mutable subclass hand back to a caller
